summary:
Echo is a browser game that runs offline. Students act as Flight Director of an Earth-observation satellite in one of three missions: tracking a hurricane from geostationary orbit, detecting wildfires from a polar orbit, or mapping a flood with an optical camera or radar.

What we developed: students choose a measurable target, then build a spacecraft within mass and budget limits. It must pass a readiness review covering the launch, space, ground and user segments before launch. They then fly 24 simulated hours through four connected challenges, such as a power fault, full storage or a short ground contact. Battery, storage, spacecraft health and unsent data carry from one challenge to the next. A final report checks each requirement, explains why it was or wasn’t met, and lets students improve the design and fly the same scenario again.

How it addresses the challenge: each decision is a real mission trade-off between data quality, power and delivery time. Simple physics simulations show students the consequences instead of telling them. Real NASA data ground the scenarios: FIRMS fire detections, GPM rainfall and OPERA flood maps.

Why it matters: students learn that a mission only succeeds when useful data reaches people on Earth in time. Shareable Mission Codes give a whole class identical, comparable conditions.
details:
TCU NASA's Project Solution

Project ECHO is an educational space mission design game that lets students do what mission engineers do: design a satellite, launch it, and fly it through a 24-hour Earth emergency. Guided by Kim, a small blue bird with solar-panel wings, players build a spacecraft within real mass and budget limits, then make the operating decisions that decide whether useful data reaches people on the ground in time. Every mission ends with a report that explains what happened and shows what real NASA satellites observed, so the game connects engineering trade-offs to NASA's open Earth data.

How Does Our Solution Work

In the game, Kim watches over Earth from orbit and asks the player for help. Each episode is a different emergency, and the player works through the same steps a real mission team follows, all from one mission room.

The player first picks a mission goal at the Earth hologram, then goes to the Workbench to build the satellite. There are five parts to choose: the instrument, the observation system, the power system, the communication system and data storage. Better parts add mass and cost, and the design has to stay inside the launch limits. The Flight Director reviews the design, and the rocket lifts off in a 3D launch sequence.

Once in orbit, the mission runs as four six-hour challenges. In each one the simulation pauses, the player makes a decision, and then watches the consequences play out in battery, storage and data delivered to Earth.

  • Storm Watch (Episode 1 · Eye of the Storm): A hurricane is heading for the coast and forecasters need fresh pictures. From geostationary orbit, the player chooses image resolution and scan area, manages storage, and then faces a Power Emergency when a fault cuts solar power to 35%. The player decides, for each two-hour period, whether to take images or save battery, and sees the predicted battery level and storm data before running the plan. The mission ends with an urgent update that must reach forecasters before hour 24.
  • Wildfire Watch (Episode 2 · The Missing Alert): A wildfire is burning near homes and the satellite only passes overhead four times. The player chooses where the heat camera looks, decides whether urgent alerts or full images go first during a one-hour ground contact, and must warn about a new hotspot within two hours of detecting it.
  • Flood Watch (Episode 3 · The Last Map): A river breaks its banks while clouds and night hide the valley. The player flies a radar satellite to map the flood anyway, works through a power anomaly in the dark, and delivers an emergency map for the town downstream.

After the fourth challenge, the Mission Report gives a score out of 100, shows which mission goals were met, lists every decision the player made, and suggests one thing to change. The report then shows real NASA observations of a similar event, clearly labelled as real and separate from the simulated mission. For Storm Watch this is a NASA GPM IMERG rainfall map from Hurricane Ian, where the heaviest rain filled under 2% of the area, which is why the choice between a wide and a focused scan matters.

Finally, the player can Rewind & Redesign: change the satellite or one decision and fly the same mission again to see what really made the difference.

The game benefits

Students, teachers and the wider community by:

  • Teaching how satellites are designed and operated, through trade-offs players can feel: mass against capability, power against imaging, storage against downlink time.
  • Showing why Earth observation matters to people, since every mission is about getting a storm image, a fire alert or a flood map to someone who needs it.
  • Building engineering habits: predict, test, read the evidence, change one thing, and try again.
  • Bridging NASA's open datasets and classroom learning, with every real observation labelled and kept separate from the simulation.
  • Supporting classrooms with Practice missions for learning the basics and Mission Codes so a whole class can fly the same conditions and compare strategies.

Our goal

To make space mission design and NASA's open Earth data accessible to students, so they understand how satellites help communities prepare for storms, wildfires and floods, and start to think like mission engineers.

The game is a teaching simulation, not a flight tool. Mission events are simulated, some numbers are simplified teaching values, and the real NASA observations are shown for comparison and do not drive the missions. It covers three kinds of emergency and does not yet include others such as drought, volcanic eruptions or sea ice.

Tools and Technologies Used

Coding Languages:

  • JavaScript, HTML and CSS → for the whole game. It runs in a web browser with nothing to install and works offline.
  • Custom simulation engines in JavaScript → one each for the storm, wildfire and flood missions. They are deterministic, so the same satellite and the same Mission Code always give the same result.
  • Three.js → for the 3D rocket and launch animation.

Data Sources:

  • NASA GPM IMERG (half-hourly rainfall, from NASA GES DISC) → the Hurricane Ian rainfall map shown in the Storm Watch report.
  • NASA FIRMS with VIIRS 375 m active-fire detections → the Maui, August 2023 fire detections shown in the Wildfire Watch report.
  • NASA/JPL OPERA DSWx-HLS (Landsat and Sentinel-2) and DSWx-S1 (Sentinel-1 radar) water maps → the central Texas, July 2025 comparison of cloud-blocked optical views and radar views shown in the Flood Watch report.
  • Published NASA and NOAA mission facts → the satellites in the game are modelled on real ones: the GOES-R series for Storm Watch (geostationary orbit at 35,786 km, 5,192 kg launch mass), NOAA-20 with VIIRS for Wildfire Watch, and NISAR for Flood Watch.
  • A Data & sources panel inside the game lists where each value comes from and marks which are real, which are published specifications, and which are simplified for teaching.

Character Design:

  • Original illustrations drawn as inline SVG → Kim, the Flight Director, the mission room and the story scenes are all vector art written in code, with no image files needed.

Use of Artificial Intelligence (AI)

Draft for the team to confirm. Keep only the lines that are true for how you worked.

We used AI tools as a supportive resource throughout the project. Specifically:

  • Design: When brainstorming game ideas, mission scenarios and interface layouts, we used AI to explore possible approaches.
  • Implementation Guidance: When uncertain about how to implement specific features, we prompted AI for coding suggestions and design best practices.
  • Debugging Assistance: During development, AI was used to help identify, explain and resolve coding errors.
  • Demo Video: Claude captured gameplay from the real game and edited the silent demo video. Kim's voice was added with TikTok AI voice.

The NASA datasets in the game were downloaded and checked by the team, and no AI-generated content is presented as NASA data.
